They were fasting, and when they set out their iftar meal to eat it, a needy person (miskīn) came, and they gave it to him. They spent the night hungry and rose the next morning fasting. Wa-laqqāhum naḍratan wa-surūrā (And He will bestow upon them radiance and joy). Al-naḍra (radiance) means luxury and comfort. This stands in contrast to the scowling of the disbeliever. The verb laqqāhum (He will bestow upon them) is among the instruments of rhetorical expression (adawāt al-bayān) [ with waqqāhum (He will shield them) in some readings ]. Bi-mā ṣabarū (﴿for what they endured with patience﴾), that is, for their patience in hunger and their preferring others over themselves, as we mentioned in the story of ʿAlī, Fāṭima, al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, may Allah be pleased with them. We have already mentioned al-arāʾik (the couches).

Lā yarawna fīhā shamsan wa-lā zamharīrā (﴿they will see therein neither sun nor bitter cold﴾): this is an expression for the moderation of its air, meaning there is neither heat nor cold in it. Al-zamharīr is severe cold. It has been said that al-zamharīr is the moon in the dialect of Ṭayy. According to this, the meaning is that Paradise has its own light, so it has no need of the sun or the moon.

Wa-dāniyatan ʿalayhim ẓilāluhā (﴿and near over them will be its shades﴾): the meaning is that the shadows of the trees hang down over them, close to them. As for the grammatical analysis (iʿrāb) of dāniyatan, it is in apposition (ʿaṭf) to muttakiʾīn (reclining). Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is in apposition to the sentence preceding it, which is lā yarawna fīhā shamsan wa-lā zamharīrā, because that sentence has the force of a single word; its estimated sense is ghayra rāʾīna fīhā shamsan wa-lā zamharīrā wa-dāniyatan (neither seeing therein sun nor bitter cold, and near). The conjunction wāw was introduced to indicate that both matters are combined for them, that is, combining distance from heat and cold with the nearness of shades. It has also been said that it is an attribute of a garden (jannah), joined by wāw as in your saying: "So-and-so is learned and righteous." It has also been said that it is in apposition to it, meaning: and another garden whose shades are near over them.

Wa-dhullilat quṭūfuhā tadhlīlā (﴿and its clusters will be made low, [hanging] in readiness﴾): al-quṭūf is the plural of qiṭf, which is a bunch of dates or grapes and the like. Its tadhlīl (making low) means that they hang down to the ground. It is reported that the people of Paradise pluck the fruits in whatever state they are, whether standing, sitting or lying down, because they hang down for them as they wish. This clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) relating to dāniyatan, meaning: near in a state in which its clusters are made low, or in apposition to it.

﴿With vessels﴾ is the plural of إناء (inā'), and its pattern is أفعلة (af'ila). We have already discussed al-akwāb (cups) in Surat al-Wāqi'ah. ﴿Crystal vessels﴾: al-qawārīr are glass (zujāj). If it is asked how they can be glass when He says ﴿of silver﴾, the answer is that what is meant is that they are originally of silver, yet resemble glass in their clarity and transparency. It is also said that they are truly of glass, and that describing them as silver is a figurative comparison, due to the nobility and whiteness of silver. Whoever reads qawārīra without tanwīn (nunation) is following the original form. Whoever reads it with tanwīn does so for the reason we explained regarding salāsil (chains).

﴿They will have measured them out with precise measure﴾ is a description of the crystal vessels. The meaning is that they were measured according to the size of the hands, or according to what the drinkers needed of the drink. Mujāhid said: "They neither diminish nor overflow." It is also said: they were measured according to what they desired. The subject pronoun in qaddarūhā may refer either to the drinkers who drink from them or to the attendants who circulate with them.

﴿Its mixture is ginger﴾: it is as we mentioned regarding its mixture being camphor (kāfūr).

﴿Salsabīl﴾: its meaning is salsal, smooth and flowing easily in its course. It is also said that it means easy to slide down the throat. It is said: sharāb salsal, salsāl and salsabīl have the same meaning. The bā' was added to the structure to intensify its smoothness, so the word became quinqueliteral (khumāsiyya). It is also said that sal is an imperative verb and sabīlan is its object, but this is extremely weak.

﴿Eternal youths﴾: this was mentioned in Surat al-Wāqi'ah.

﴿Like scattered pearls﴾: He likened them to pearls in beauty and whiteness, and to scattered pearls in their numbers and their dispersal throughout the palaces.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 76, verses 27–31:

﴿Indeed, these love the immediate (world)﴾: that is, the worldly life (al-dunya). The pointing (al-ishara) is to the disbelievers, and "the heavy day" is the Day of Resurrection. Describing it as "heavy" is an expression for its terror (hawl) and severity (shidda).

﴿And We strengthened their makeup﴾: al-asr means the physical make-up (al-khilqa). It was also said: the joints and the articulations (al-mafasil wa'l-awsal). And it was said: the strength (al-quwwa).

﴿We have replaced their likes with a (complete) replacement﴾: that is, We destroyed them and replaced them with others. It was also said: We transformed them, changing their forms, and this is a threat.

﴿Indeed, this is a reminder﴾: the pointing is to the verse, or the surah, or the Law (al-shari'a) in its entirety.

﴿So whoever wills﴾: this is an exhortation (tahdid) and an encouragement (targhib). Then He restricted their will by the will of God.

﴿And the wrongdoers﴾: this is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb whose estimated form is: "and He punishes the wrongdoers."
